passages.text: Lost lovers linked at long last: elusive female <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> mystery solved after a century of being placed in a different genus (Phasmatodea, Phylliidae)
Abstract

After successful laboratory rearing of both males and females from a single clutch of eggs, the genus <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> Redtenbacher, 1906 (described only from males) and the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group within Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) Griffini, 1898 (described only from females) are found to be the opposite sexes of the same genus. <sentence_start/>This rearing observation finally elucidates the relationship of these two small body sized leaf insect groups which, for more than a century, have never been linked before. <sentence_start/>This paper synonymizes the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group with <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> Redtenbacher, 1906 in order to create a singular and clearly defined taxonomic group. <sentence_start/>Five species are transferred from the Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) frondosum species group and create the following new combinations: <italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> (Größer, 2002), <bold>comb. nov.</bold>; <italic>Nanophylliumchitoniscoides</italic> (Größer, 1992), <bold>comb. nov.</bold>; <italic>Nanophylliumfrondosum</italic> (Redtenbacher, 1906), <bold>comb. nov.</bold>; <italic>Nanophylliumkeyicum</italic> (Karny, 1914), <bold>comb. nov.</bold>; <italic>Nanophylliumsuzukii</italic> (Größer, 2008), <bold>comb. nov.</bold> <sentence_start/>The only taxon from this species group not transferred from the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group to <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> is Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) groesseri Zompro, 1998. <sentence_start/>Based on protibial exterior lobes, this species belongs in the <italic>schultzei</italic> species group as described in <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11646/zootaxa.2322.1.1" count="1">Hennemann et al. 2009</citation> and is therefore excluded from further discussion here. <sentence_start/>The rearing of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> also yielded the male <italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> (Größer, 2002), <bold>comb. nov.</bold> thus, enabling comparison of this male to the other previously known <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species. <sentence_start/>Two new species of nano-leaf insects are described within, <italic>Nanophylliummiyashitai</italic><bold>sp. nov.</bold>, from Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea, and <italic>Nanophylliumdaphne</italic><bold>sp. nov.</bold>, from Biak Island, Papua Province, Indonesia. <sentence_start/>With such distinct sexual dimorphism in <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> between sexes, which have only now been matched up via captive rearing, illustrated within are numerous specimens which might represent the unknown opposite sexes of the many currently known species of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>. <sentence_start/>Due to pronounced sexual dimorphism in <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>, only future captive rearing or molecular analysis will match up the many unknown sexes. <sentence_start/>To conclude, with the description of two new <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species, dichotomous keys to species for known males and females are presented.
Introduction

The leaf insects (Phylliidae) represent a lineage within the stick insects (Phasmatodea), which are popular as pets and within insect collections due to their impressive leaf-like camouflage. <sentence_start/>The Phylliidae have an impressive array of morphological adaptations to mimic different types of leaves. <sentence_start/>Present in many species is the ability for various color forms which allow them to look like living, dying, or dead leaves (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>These masters of leaf-like camouflage can be found throughout Southeast Asia, with some of the biodiversity hotspots being Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Brock et al. 2020</citation>).
Figure 1.
Live <italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> (Größer, 2002), comb. nov. <sentence_start/>females, three primary color forms photographed in Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea.

Included within the Phylliidae are the <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> Redtenbacher, 1906 a group of small bodied species which for more than 100 years have only been known from rarely collected male specimens. <sentence_start/>Throughout a majority of those years only the single type species <italic>Nanophylliumpygmaeum</italic> Redtenbacher, 1906 was recognized. <sentence_start/>It was not until the last couple of decades that a majority of new <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species began to be described (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Brock et al. 2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>With numerous species described throughout the island of New Guinea solely from male specimens, the question begs to be asked, “where are the female <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>?”. <sentence_start/>Could the lack of females be that they are incredibly elusive, or already well-known and simply not recognized as female <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>?

<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1665/1082-6467(2002)011[0199:SOTLIP]2.0.CO;2" count="1">Brock and Hasenpusch (2003</citation>: 203, fig. 6) were the first to suggest and illustrate the unknown <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> female, an individual from Nabire, Irian Jaya, collected along with a male which would later become the holotype of <italic>Nanophylliumhasenpuschi</italic> Brock & Größer, 2008. <sentence_start/>Unfortunately, however, the female specimen is missing both front legs (an important morphological identification feature frequently used for differentiation) but all other features place it morphologically close to Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) frondosum Redtenbacher, 1909. <sentence_start/>Additionally, <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1665/1082-6467(2002)011[0199:SOTLIP]2.0.CO;2" count="1">Brock and Hasenpusch (2003)</citation> discuss the subadult female found by G. B. Monteith in 1971 in the Iron Range, Queensland as additional evidence that a “<italic>frondosum</italic>-like species” is probably the unknown female for the <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>. <sentence_start/>As it turns out, the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group, as defined by <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11646/zootaxa.2322.1.1" count="1">Hennemann et al. (2009)</citation>, are also somewhat of a quandary since they are only known from female specimens, except for Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) groesseri Zompro, 1998. <sentence_start/>In light of the speculation by <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1665/1082-6467(2002)011[0199:SOTLIP]2.0.CO;2" count="1">Brock and Hasenpusch (2003)</citation> the authors scoured major collections around the world for additional <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> male specimens and females of the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group looking for shared morphological features which might support the thoughts of <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1665/1082-6467(2002)011[0199:SOTLIP]2.0.CO;2" count="1">Brock and Hasenpusch (2003)</citation>.

As it so happens, the breakthrough was not due to the exhaustive review of museum specimens, but instead came as a surprise at the Montreal Insectarium, Quebec, Canada. <sentence_start/>In April 2018 the Insectarium received eggs of Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) asekiense Größer, 2002 from Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea with the hopes of raising this beautifully variable species in captivity (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>The surprise came in early 2019 when the three sole survivors of the very slow developing nymphs reached adulthood; as one female <italic>Phylliumasekiense</italic> and two male ‘<italic>Nanophyllium</italic>’. <sentence_start/>This breakthrough at long last was the evidence we had been searching for to remove the speculation of these two known, but never associated, taxa.

This pairing of the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group with the <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> morphologically was not surprising given numerous morphological similarities between the taxonomic groups (discussed below). <sentence_start/>From our extensive review of museum specimens, we found males ranging in length from ~ 27 to 40 mm and females ranging from ~ 46 to 71 mm, a difference which is not outside of the norm with the male to female ratio seen throughout the family.
Materials and methods

The holotype specimen of <italic>Nanophylliummiyashitai</italic> sp. nov. was loaned to the Montreal Insectarium (Stéphane Le Tirant, collection manager) from the extensive collection of Tetsuo Miyashita, Japan. <sentence_start/>See the abbreviations section below for a full list of collections (both institutional and large private) in which relevant material was recovered.

Photos of specimens that were loaned to/held within the Montreal Insectarium were taken by René Limoges of using a Nikon D810 DSLR camera with Nikon Micro-Nikkor 200 mm f/4 lens on Manfrotto 454 micrometric positioning sliding plate. <sentence_start/>Lighting was provided by two Nikon SB-25 flash units with a Cameron Digital diffusion photo box. <sentence_start/>Adobe Photoshop Elements 13 was used as post processing software. <sentence_start/>The <italic>Nanophylliummiyashitai</italic> sp. nov. <sentence_start/>holotype specimen is deposited in the Montreal Insectarium (Quebec, Canada) type collection.

Photographs of the female <italic>Nanophylliumchitoniscoides</italic> (Größer, 1992) comb. nov. <sentence_start/>(Fig. 16A) were taken by Frank Hennemann within his personal collection using a Nikon D7000 camera equipped with a Nikon DX AF-S Micro 40 mm lens and a wireless Nikon SU-800 dual speed light system. <sentence_start/>Background lightning was provided by a 18W 6000K LED panel light plate.

The photograph of the female holotype <italic>Nanophylliumsuzukii</italic> (Größer, 2008) comb. nov. <sentence_start/>(Fig. 16B) was taken by Mandy Schröter under direction of Stephan Blanke at the Senckenberg German Entomological Institute Müncheberg using a Nikon D7200 digital camera and a Nikon Micro Nikkor 105 mm f/2.8 G ED objective. <sentence_start/>Lightning was from the Yongnuo Digital Speedlight YN 560 IV reflected by the inner surface of a Styrofoam box set up around the specimen. <sentence_start/>A grey card was used for white balance. <sentence_start/>Composite images with an extended depth of field were created using the software StackShot Macro Rail Package (Cognisys Inc., U.S.A.) and Zerene Stacker (release November 7, 2017; Zerene Systems LLC, U.S.A.).

Results
Captive rearing of Nanophyllium in the Montreal Insectarium

In January 2018, Stéphane Le Tirant of the Montreal Insectarium applied for a live insect import permit from the CFIA to allow the importation of live eggs to Canada from local insect suppliers in Papua New Guinea. <sentence_start/>Fortunately, one of those suppliers was able to export a small series of eggs freshly laid by a wild caught female <italic>Phylliumasekiense</italic>, collected in Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. <sentence_start/>In April 2018, the Montreal Insectarium received 13 eggs, all black in color, and with the same morphology across the series. <sentence_start/>Eggs were incubated at room temperature on a plastic screen mesh within a plastic box with coco fiber at the base which was regularly sprayed with water to maintain humidity. <sentence_start/>Of these thirteen received eggs, during a period of seven to eleven months only five nymphs hatched (Fig. 2D). <sentence_start/>In an attempt to find at least one species of food which the fresh nymphs would accept, nymphs were offered <italic>Psidiumguajava</italic> (Guava), <italic>Rubus</italic> sp. (Bramble), and <italic>Gaultheriashallon</italic> (Salal) to eat. <sentence_start/>These three plants are commonly accepted host plants regularly used within the Montreal Insectarium.
Figure 2.

Live <italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> (Größer, 2002), comb. nov. raised in the Montreal Insectarium <bold>A</bold> subadult female, full body dorsal <bold>B</bold> subadult female, head and front legs, dorsal <bold>C</bold> adult male, full body dorsal <bold>D</bold> freshly hatched nymph <bold>E</bold> nymph, later instar.

Of these five nymphs, two nymphs refuse to eat any of the host plants offered entirely and died within a few days. <sentence_start/>The other three nymphs thankfully accepted bramble and during the first few instars all three individuals looked very similar in morphology (Fig. 2E). <sentence_start/>All three nymphs were quite active both day and night and fed continuously. <sentence_start/>It was not until the last two molts that the sexual dimorphism became noticeable, and after a period of 90 to 130 days after first hatching all three reached adulthood as two males and one female. <sentence_start/>Unfortunately, the males became adult (Fig. 2C) whilst the female was still only a subadult (Fig. 2A). <sentence_start/>The males were active by day and night (readily flying) and lived only for about four months, dying before the female was adult.

The female lived as an adult for about nine months before dying, producing a total of 245 eggs of many different colors (Fig. 3). <sentence_start/>During the peak of her egg producing life she produced three to four eggs per day, and as many as 112 eggs in a single month. <sentence_start/>In adulthood, the female was no longer active during the day and only fed at night. <sentence_start/>In the months since the 245 eggs were laid, they have been incubating and during this period very few nymphs have successfully hatched, and all refused to feed on the three host plant species that were offered and accepted by the original culture. <sentence_start/>To try and ensure that the species was successfully brought into culture, the Montreal Insectarium shared many eggs with other experienced Phylliidae breeders but they also were unsuccessful with obtaining a subsequent generation.
Figure 3.

<italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> (Größer, 2002), comb. nov. eggs laid by the single adult female which made it to adulthood in the Montreal Insectarium; note the variability of color within the eggs laid by this singular female.

Despite the failed attempt to bring this species into culture, the successful rearing of both sexes from a batch of eggs from a single female has allowed the much needed definitive evidence to back up the morphological observations that the females of the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group and the males of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> are simply one and the same. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group of Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) is here transferred to the genus <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> (except for <italic>Ph.groesseri</italic>, which instead belongs to the Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) schultzei species group based in the protibial lobes and is therefore left within the Phyllium (Pulchriphyllium) subgenus). <sentence_start/>The genus <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> is here revised with most species illustrated and a general description for the male, female, and egg morphology after more than 100 years is now summarized together.

a. <sentence_start/>In the smallest species (individuals ~ 56.0 mm or less), the radial bend occurs before the splitting of the first radial and the radial sector, therefore the radial sector is straight (for example see <italic>N.chitoniscoides</italic> comb. nov.; Fig. 8A). <sentence_start/>These females also have a radius and medial crossvein present on the radial bend at or before the splitting of the first radial (Fig. 8A). <sentence_start/>The cubitus at its terminus is clearly split into the anterior cubitus and posterior cubitus veins with a clearly defined gap between them (Fig. 8A). <sentence_start/>Example species are <italic>N.chitoniscoides</italic> comb. nov., <italic>N.daphne</italic> sp. nov.

b. <sentence_start/>For the larger species, the bend in the radial vein happens on the radial sector after the splitting of the first radial from the radius (Fig. 8B). <sentence_start/>Also, the radius and medial crossvein occurs after the splitting of the first radial, instead originating on the radial sector (Fig. 8B). <sentence_start/>The cubitus at its terminus can be weakly split into the anterior cubitus and posterior cubitus, but in many specimens this vein is simple and unbranched (it is never clearly split with a large gap between the anterior cubitus and posterior cubitus like is seen in the smaller species; Fig. 8A). <sentence_start/>Example species are <italic>N.asekiense</italic> comb. nov., <italic>N.frondosum</italic> comb. nov., or <italic>N.suzukii</italic> comb. nov.

c. <sentence_start/>The final venation pattern is found in <italic>Nanophylliumkeyicum</italic> comb. nov., the only species in this genus which has a wide gap between the media and cubitus veins which persists throughout the entire length of the media, this gap is several times wider than a single vein width. <sentence_start/>This feature is only seen on this species from Kei Island, Indonesia (Fig. 8C). <sentence_start/>All other examined <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species have the media and cubitus veins running side by side throughout the entire length, no farther than a single vein width apart (for example in the larger species like <italic>N.asekiense</italic> comb. nov. or <italic>N.suzukii</italic> comb. nov.; Fig. 8B), or with veins moderately wide for the anterior portion (at most two or three vein widths apart) but as they reach the splitting of the media posterior the width between the media and cubitus veins is reduced and the veins are side by side (this example can be seen in the smaller species like <italic>N.daphne</italic> sp. nov.). <sentence_start/>Also, in <italic>N.keyicum</italic> comb. nov., the radius and medial crossvein occurs after the splitting of the first radial, instead originating on the radial sector (Fig. 8C). <sentence_start/>Similar to the larger species, the cubitus at its terminus can be weakly split into the anterior cubitus and posterior cubitus (like those seen in Fig. 8B), but in most specimens of <italic>N.keyicum</italic> comb. nov. <sentence_start/>this vein is simple and unbranched (as illustrated in Fig. 8C).

Male <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> general morphology

The <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> based on male morphology can be separated into two distinct species groups, the <italic>pygmaeum</italic> species group (Fig. 10A) and the <italic>stellae</italic> species group (Fig. 10B). <sentence_start/>Males of several species for the two species groups are known, but females and eggs are only known for the <italic>pygmaeum</italic> species group, the female and eggs are not yet known for the <italic>stellae</italic> species group.
Figure 10.

Side by side <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> males of the two species groups <bold>A</bold><italic>pygmaeum</italic> species group, <italic>Nanophylliumasekiense</italic> male from Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea <bold>B</bold><italic>stellae</italic> species group, <italic>Nanophylliumstellae</italic> HT from Jayapura, Indonesia.

Easily observed morphological features which differentiate the species groups are the femoral lobes. <sentence_start/>The <italic>pygmaeum</italic> species group has profemoral interior lobes which are angular (Fig. 11D-H) and mesofemoral interior lobes which do not reach from end to end of the shaft and have distinct serrate teeth. <sentence_start/>The <italic>stellae</italic> species group has profemoral interior lobes which are rounded without a sharp angle (Fig. 11A-C) and mesofemoral interior lobes which are a large rounded triangle, reaching from end to end without prominent spination.

This small species (body length of the holotype only 54.0 mm) has several interesting morphological features which differentiate it from other known <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> females. <sentence_start/>The tegmina venation places this species most closely aligned to <italic>N.chitoniscoides</italic> due to the venation pattern having the radial bend occurring before the splitting of the first radial and the radial sector, therefore the radial sector is straight (Fig. 9A). <sentence_start/>Additionally, a radial and medial crossvein is present on the radial bend at or before the splitting of the first radial (Fig. 9A).

This new species can be differentiated from all other <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> by several morphological features. <sentence_start/>First, it is the only species which has exterior profemoral lobes which are obtuse (Fig. 21A), not right angles like in <italic>N.keyicum</italic> (Fig. 16D) or recurved acute angles like in all other known <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species (for example Fig. 16C). <sentence_start/>Additionally, this is the only species known where the female has the abdomen tapering towards the posterior, giving the abdomen a spade-shaped appearance (Fig. 21C), all other known species have females with abdominal segments VI and VII either parallel sided (like in <italic>N.frondosum</italic> and <italic>N.keyicum</italic>, Fig. 16C, D respectively) or as the broadest segments (like in <italic>N.chitoniscoides</italic> and <italic>N.suzukii</italic>, Fig. 16A, B, respectively).

<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fevo.2018.00216" count="1">Robertson et al. 2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>The report of the fossil <italic>Eophylliummesselense</italic> Wedmann, Bradler & Rust, 2007 gives further indication that Phylliidae arose more than 47 mya ago and estimates the splitting of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> from the remaining Phylliidae ~ 20 mya ago (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0606937104" pmid="17197423" pmcid="PMC1766425" count="1">Wedmann et al. 2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Assuming an approximate splitting of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> 20-35 mya from the remaining Phylliidae some conclusions on the biogeographical history of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> can be drawn. <sentence_start/>Ancestors of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> probably settled New Guinea close to that timeframe, after New Guinea emerged in the Eocene (~ 40 mya) and was separated from Australia during the Oligocene (~25 mya) after the New Guinea Passive Margin collided with the leading edge of the Eastern Philippines-Halmahera-New Guinea Arc System (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Hall 2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>As extant phylliids inhabit most parts of the Oriental and Australian region, but <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>, so far known, is restricted to New Guinea, including the surrounding islands, and Australia (Fig. 4), this lineage probably evolved on New Guinea and later migrated to northern Australia. <sentence_start/><italic>Nanophyllium</italic> likely diversified on New Guinea due to geographic isolation by the Central Cordillera (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Chisholm 1911</citation>) and the Foja Mountain Ranges in the north (<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11646/zootaxa.2277.1.1" count="1">Richards et al. 2009</citation>; <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11646/zootaxa.4671.1.9" count="1">Oliver et al. 2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>During the Pleistocene (2.6 mya-11.7 ka) Australia and New Guinea were interconnected many times, due to climatic oscillation resulting in sea level fluctuations (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0037-0738(98)00095-5" count="1">Pillans et al. 1998</citation>), but the remaining parts of Indonesia remained separated from New Guinea (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jbi.12416" count="1">Ludt and Rocha 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>The southernmost population of <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> possibly distributed to Australia and became separated, resulting in the speciation of <italic>N.pygmaeum</italic> and <italic>N.australianum</italic> after the Last Glacial Maximum ~ 17-19 ka ago (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jbi.12416" count="1">Ludt and Rocha 2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>The distributional records of the known <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> specimens suggest a well-established isolation of the distributions of <italic>N.miyashitai</italic> sp. nov. <sentence_start/>from other <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> by the Central Cordillera. <sentence_start/>As this formation arose quite early (probably during the Oligocene (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" count="1">Hall 2001</citation>), this population potentially has been isolated for a comparatively long time, that likely led to allopatric speciation. <sentence_start/>Likewise, most of the other <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> species are probably a result of allopatric isolation caused by this mountain range. <sentence_start/><italic>Nanophylliumkeyicum</italic> and <italic>N.daphne</italic> sp. nov. <sentence_start/>in contrast, are probably a result of the isolation on the islands they are found, which became separated from mainland New Guinea.

Conclusions

Review of a wide number of institution and private collections as well as the successful rearing by the Montreal Insectarium has revealed the identity of a previously unconfirmed female <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>. <sentence_start/>This has allowed us to synonymize the <italic>frondosum</italic> species group (only known from females) with the <italic>Nanophyllium</italic> (only known from males) into a single genus.

Unfortunately, due to the striking sexual dimorphism in <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>, this leaves many females and males with unknown opposite sexes and the possibility that some of the presently described species of either group might simply be the opposite sex of an already known species. <sentence_start/>Hopefully future collections of fresh material from throughout the region will either allow successful rearing of species to elucidate the unknown sex or allow pairing of sexes on a molecular basis. <sentence_start/>Additionally, we eagerly await extensive molecular analysis for the Phylliidae as a whole to elucidate the higher taxonomy within the family and the placement of the <italic>Nanophyllium</italic>.
